data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, methodological decision to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, provided one accepts that this preference guarantees no future success and incurs the cost of abandoning any claim to rational expectation of truth or predictive reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a guarantee or even a probabilistic likelihood that the preferred theory will succeed in novel domains, the Popperian defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'rational action' inherently requires an inductive bridge between past tests and future applications, the preference smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent cannot accept the cost of acting without expectation (i.e., treating the choice as a blind guess that happens to be the least-bad option), the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Critical Preferential Volition': scientists voluntarily adopt the best-tested theory not because it is probable or likely true (which would be induction), but because it is the only one that has not yet been eliminated by logic. This transforms preference from an epistemic judgment about the future into a logical status report about the past, where acting on the unrefuted is the only rational move consistent with the aim of finding truth, even if the link between past survival and future performance remains logically unjustified.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
